result:
**None of the three answers appears correct.** Solution 1 is the least wrong, since it agrees with my best check at k = 4.

**Reformulation.** For a k-set S, G[S] must be K_{1,k-1} itself, or else have no vertex adjacent to all others in S (so it does not contain the star) and not have all its edges through one vertex (so it is not a subgraph of the star).

**Solution 1 (2k−2) is refuted for k = 5.** Take three disjoint copies of K₄, which has 12 vertices against the claimed maximum of 8. An induced 5-vertex subgraph is K_a + K_b + K_c with a+b+c = 5 and each part at most 4. Since no part has size 5, no vertex has degree 4, so the star is not contained. If some part has size ≥3 there is a triangle; if two parts have size ≥2 there are two disjoint edges. Either way the graph is not contained in a star. The only remaining pattern (2,1,1,…) would need sum at least 5 with at most one part of size 2, which is impossible with three parts. So the graph is K_{1,4}-exact with 12 > 8 vertices. The upper-bound argument in Solution 1 is also not valid as written.

**Solution 2 (answer 4) is refuted.** K_{3,3} is K_{1,3}-exact: its 4-vertex induced subgraphs are K_{1,3}, C₄, or K_{3,1}, all allowed. That gives 6 > 4.

**Solution 3 (k² − k + 1 = 13 at k = 4) is refuted.** For k = 4, the forbidden induced 4-vertex graphs include K₄, the diamond, the paw, P₃+K₁, K₂+2K₁, and 4K₁. Any triangle must then be a whole connected component. Combined with R(3,4) = 9 and α ≤ 3, this bounds |V(G)| well below 13.

For k = 4, the bound above is consistent with a maximum of 6, which matches Solution 1 and the construction 2K₃. I did not establish the true general formula. The 3K₄ construction suggests (k−1)(k−2) as a lower bound for general k, but I have not proved it is optimal.

CHOICE: 1
